newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania splits largest state-owned bank in three.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania splits largest state-owned bank in three.

text.p: Tanzania's largest state-owned bank will be split in three as part of reforms of the financial sector, a senior central bank official told Reuters on Tuesday.
Reform of the National Bank of Commerce (NBC), which controls over 70 percent of the banking sector, will be carried out within the next six months.

The NBC, established in 1967 under sweeping socialist policies, has 172 branches across this impoverished east African nation. It operates as a semi-autonomous bank although the government is the sole shareholder.

"The National Bank of Commerce is a very big bank and it controls over 70 percent of the banking sector here. Its action very much influences all the commercial banks and sometimes it even influences monetary policies in the wrong direction," the official told Reuters.
He said that splitting the NBC into three smaller banks -- a trade bank, a regional rural bank and a bank for micro-finance -- would improve the overall standard of banking in Tanzania.
"The competition in the commercial banking sector will be more fair and it will help reduce the monopoly power the NBC had, while at the same time capitalise it and make it more profitable," he said.
The official said a task force would set up the three smaller banks within the next six months.
The NBC has incurred huge losses for a long time. Bank officials say the government and state-owned enterprises are mainly responsible for the bad debts.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) resident representative in Tanzania welcomed the news of the split, describing it as a major step forward that will create a sound local banking sector in the country.
"In our view it's a very positive development and it's a major policy commitment under the Enhanced Structual Adjustment Facility (ESAF)," Festus Osunsade told Reuters.
The IMF approved the $234 million three-year ESAF to Tanzania last November, marking the return of IMF support to Tanzania for the first time since 1992.

"We see this as part of what is needed for orienting the banking sector here into a competitive multi-tier banking system. As recently as six months ago the NBC had 78 percent of total deposits of all the banks in Tanzania so it was really the price setter.

"There was no freely competitive market in the banking sector, but now, with the bank divided into three, each of the units will at the most have 20 to 30 percent and whatever it does it cannot be the deciding factor," Osunsade said.

He said another important factor in the coming split of the NBC was that it would help the government phase out the need to use budgetary resources to bail out the NBC, as happened on several occasions in the past.
"This is a big plus and it's very important because it will remove this burden from the back of the government," he said.
Reforming the NBC was one of the conditions demanded by the IMF for it to release more funds to Tanzania.
Other conditions include IMF demands that Tanzania control central bank borrowing, limit government spending and increase revenue collection.
The central bank official said that once NBC is split it could lead to a more competitive market which would encourage more foreign banks to seek business in Tanzania.
